deep.reconstruction:
PART A (end of the remark 'Bemerkung zu meiner Methode der unabhängigen Integrale', continued from the previous page). Setting: minimise J = ∫_Ω F(x,y,z,z_x,z_y) dω. Hilbert's independent (invariant) integral is J* = ∫_Ω {F(x,y,z,p,q) + (z_x − p)F_p + (z_y − q)F_q} dω, where p(x,y,z), q(x,y,z) is a slope field. In the original method one demands that J* depend only on the boundary values of z. This turns the requirement into partial differential equations for p and q, namely the field equations, equivalently the Euler–Lagrange equation for the field. The remark replaces this with a weaker demand: J*[z̃] ≥ J*[z] for every z̃ with the same boundary values as the given z. The PDEs then become partial differential inequalities. Hilbert says the same chain of conclusions as before still goes through. In the end the criterion requires only the solution of a boundary value problem for PDEs. The method amounts to arranging the (p,q)-field so that the given z minimises J*. This is a sufficiency or field-embedding statement in Weierstrass–Hilbert style; it is only sketched and no computation is given.

PART B (programmatic remark). The usual calculus of variations asks only how to choose a function so that a minimum occurs. In differential calculus, the minimum of a function is just one special question. Likewise the calculus of variations should be a general theory of relations between two variable functions y(x), z(x), just as function theory or differential calculus is a theory of relations between two variable quantities y, z.

The simplest such relations are those given by 'diophantine', i.e. ordinary, differential equations f(x, y, z, dy/dx, dz/dx, …) = 0. A single equation for two unknown functions is underdetermined. These are the analogue of algebraic relations between quantities. The analogue of the uniformisation problem is the 'integral-free' (integrallos) representation of all solutions of f = 0. This means x, y, z given as fixed functions of t, w(t), w'(t), …, w^(n)(t), with w arbitrary and no quadratures. The next page adds that integral-free solvable equations are the analogue of genus-0 curves, which can be rationalised.

Test example: x^2 d²y/dx² = dz/dx. Write it in parametric form with ' = d/dt:
- d²y/dx² = (x'y'' − y'x'')/x'^3
- dz/dx = z'/x'
- Hence x^2(x'y'' − y'x'') = z'x'^2, exactly as written.

One then seeks x, y, z = Funktion(t, w, w', …, w^(n)) making this an identity in the independent symbols t, w, …, w^(n+2). The last line says the linear diophantine (Pfaffian) equation is in any case solvable this way; this is continued on the next page.

Footnote: the simplest example is x'y' = s'^2. It is homogeneous of degree 2 in d/dt, so it is reparametrisation-invariant: dx·dy = ds^2. The proposed solution is x = e^t(w'' − w'), y = e^{−t}(w'' + w'), s = w + w''.
- [mine] Differentiating: x' = e^t(w''' − w') and y' = e^{−t}(w''' − w').
- [mine] Hence x'y' = (w''' − w')^2.
- [mine] This requires s' = ±(w''' − w'), i.e. s = w'' − w (or w − w''), not w + w''.

The idea is the germ of Hilbert's 1912 paper 'Über den Begriff der Klasse von Differentialgleichungen'.
errors: Footnote: with x = e^t(w''−w') and y = e^{−t}(w''+w') one gets x'y' = (w'''−w')^2. However, s = w + w'' gives s'^2 = (w'+w''')^2, so the identity fails. The sign must be s = w'' − w (or w − w''). This is a sign slip.

Not an error, but worth noting [mine]: the proposed 'simple example' x^2 y'' = z' is linear in z' and y''. It is trivially integral-free solvable: x = t, y = w', z = t^2 w'' − 2t w' + 2w. It therefore cannot serve as an example of impossibility. Hilbert's published counterexample (1912) is the nonlinear z' = (y'')^2.
Part A is only asserted ('the same conclusions can be drawn'). There is no argument that the differential inequalities reduce to the same boundary value problem.

results.what: Replacing the independence requirement on the invariant integral J* by a minimality requirement (PDE → partial differential inequalities), reducing the sufficiency criterion to a boundary value problem.
results.modern_name: Hilbert invariant integral / Weierstrass field theory sufficiency (field-embedding) for multiple integrals

results.what: Programme: view the calculus of variations as a theory of relations between functions; underdetermined ODEs as analogues of algebraic relations; the 'uniformisation' analogue is integral-free parametrisation of all solutions.
results.modern_name: Integral-free solution (Hilbert–Cartan), differential flatness; Monge problem

results.what: Parametric integral-free solution of the Monge equation x'y' = s'^2 via an arbitrary function w and its derivatives.
results.modern_name: Flat parametrisation of a Monge equation
results.usually_credited_to: Monge / Hilbert 1912 (Monge equations are integral-free solvable)

results.what: Parametric form x^2(x'y''−y'x'') = z'x'^2 of x^2 y'' = z' as a test case for integral-free representation.
results.modern_name: Reparametrisation-invariant form of an underdetermined ODE

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft precursor of Hilbert's published 1912 notion of integral-free solvability and its genus-0/uniformisation analogy, which is already credited to him. The 'diophantine ODE' terminology and the variational motivation are a nice unpublished framing, but not a new result.
